utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stamp. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Chairman -- Mr. President, if I may. Thank you. The Defence would like to make a very brief preliminary statement. It will take a couple of minutes maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I would like to make it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would be in relation to the expert reports, I would deal with this after this witness, but if it is something different, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in relation to the procedure in general, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence counsel has met, not just the two people that you have in front of you, but the entire team, and we felt it would be useful to make the following statement: In no way would we like to start harping on to interlogical matters, but we believe that, apart from all interpretation problems and apart from any confusion which might be created here and there, depending on various elements cropping up in the course of this procedure, and quite apart from all the other problems, the Defence would like to state quite clearly that we have never heard and that we have never tried, and have never intended, to consider this courtroom and any other courtroom of this Tribunal as a playground. I believe it is very important for the Defence to make this statement loud and clear. More than anything else, we want to act as the Defence of the accused. We are fully aware of the stakes within this institution, so never in the past, never in the future and never at the present can we consider any part of this procedure as our playground, because the procedure is far too important to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me give you just as brief an answer as you expressed yourself briefly. When I used these words yesterday, it was at the occasion when the Chamber was provided with a page which was entirely black. I do understand that this was a mistake, and the Chamber accepts that it was a mistake and that there were no bad intentions behind it. Mr. Stamp, are you ready to resume the examination of the witness, Mr. Grebic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then, please, Mr. Usher, lead the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, please be seated. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you made yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last time we spoke, you told us that you were taken to the hospital where you were treated. Were you admitted or discharged from the hospital that day?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was hospitalized for five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And after that, did you return for treatment?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went every other day to have my wounds re-bandaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, Your Honours, may I tender to the witness document P1517B, and to the Court P1517B and P1517B1, which is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Once again, it would appear that the Defence has not received that translation, and apparently it is just a draft, if I am correct in reading the first two words. So it is the draft translation, not the final one. And we did ask for such a document yesterday and we haven't been given it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, could you please respond on the question of the Defence why there is just a draft translation and not a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What we are trying to do, at great effort and expense of resources, is to reconcile the translations we have had with the B/C/S document and, in some cases, provide what we consider to be further translations. So notwithstanding that this document is noted as a draft translation, we tender it as the best translation we have of the exhibit itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If at one moment you could provide whatever kind of confirmation that this draft translation is a correct translation, it would be highly appreciated. At this very moment, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, since you read both languages, apart from the Latin, as far as I understand, is there any point of specific concern in relation to the draft translation provided to you at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Audiens sapiens, Mr. President. As a consequence, I am obliged to reply to you what I am a bit surprised about. I am unable to read the name. And the Latin used to say "nomen est omen," everything is in the name. And I can see another name which is crossed out there and I don't see why. I can see that, once again, we have got the problem of stamps and seals here. They seem to be itinerant seals since they are to the right and used to be on the other side and, once again, they are not translated. So I'm still rather surprised, and I suppose I am going to stay that way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, the seal seems to have been translated. At least, the last part of the draft translation reads: "Seal, General Hospital, Dobrinja, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are quite right. It is a round seal that we can see down at the bottom, apparently, but it also appears that there is a rectangular one to the right side of the document a bit higher up and, apparently, that one has not been translated. I think it might be a seal, but I can't tell because I haven't seen the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you inspected the most original version in the hands of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, but if it is submitted to us, we will do so with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then those parts legible, is there any specific concern about the translation in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since I have only just received the translation, may I have a couple of minutes to read through it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is any specific concern, please inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's do it like that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document? Can you identify it?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this document and I can confirm what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the letter on the basis of which I was discharged from the hospital, from Dobrinja Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the top of this document, do you see your name there, your surname written in hand?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Name and surname, the name of the doctor who put the seal on this letter. He actually made a mistake in that he misspelled the first letter in -- of my name. When I took this letter, before leaving, I warned her. I said that it was a "D" instead of a "G" and so she crossed it out and spelled my name correctly, and it is handwritten. You can see it quite clearly, when I was admitted, how long I was hospitalized and when I was discharged. You can see the date of discharge and the date of admission. And I don't know what else I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, tell us, you see "Tesanj" to the top right of the document?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you see the figures "1946"?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the year in which I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And above that, after your surname, do you see a name, "Asir," in brackets?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is written on the document. That is my father's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And below that, do you see "E. Zola 7"? Can you see what that is?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the name of the street where I was living. The full name would be the street of Emile Zola, number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may take you back to the day that you were injured. You had travelled to your sister's house to visit her. Do you remember how you travelled? Was it by car, by foot, by bicycle? By what means did you travel?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you remember what the weather was like on the scene of where this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As weather conditions go, it was changing. I don't know exactly remember what time it was, but sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you said it was changing. Changing from what to what?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was partly sunny and partly cloudy and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that when you arrived there, you were making small talk with a woman, Dragica, who was at the gate. Can you remember her full name?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She was a friend, a friend of my sister's, Semsa. She had been a family friend even before Bosnia-Herzegovina and I met her at my sister's place, and I knew her name was Dragica Micanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did she live in that community?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She lived in the so-called airport settlement which was occupied by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What ethnicity was she, do you know?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was Serbian by nationality

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to her in this shelling incident on the 12th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to it front door of the house where my sister was staying, after a couple of seconds, this shell landed and Mrs. Dragica lost her life, as many other civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the position, at the place where this incident occurred, do you know of any military facility nearby at that time?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to correct you. It was not an incident, it was a massacre. There were no military facilities in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how far the closest Bosnian army lines were?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian army lines and the Serb army lines were to the south-east of that building and about 500 metres away. That is in the direction of the airport settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you ever heard or do you know of a tunnel which was built from Dobrinja, running under the airport to Butmir?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say, if you know, when that tunnel came into operation or approximately when?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of July 1993, when this terrible massacre happened, the tunnel was being dug, in the process of being dug. In came into operation by the end of November or beginning of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall any other shelling incidents in that same vicinity before or after the incident of the 12th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that incident, I can't remember, and after that particular massacre, other shells landed, in that area, in the same area where that particular massacre took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say, "in the same area," about how far from the gate with the pump?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately five to six days later, another shell landed to the right of the gate, right in the middle of the road and there was -- it left a big mark. Then my sister Semsa was actually in the courtyard and she was basically still cleaning up after the previous massacre. Since the courtyard is lower than the street level, a piece of shrapnel hit her in the head, but it was just a superficial injury and so it only took away some of her hair and she was not killed or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The place where this shell fell a few days after the 12th of July, about how far did it impact from the gate?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 45 metres, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in your experience, does a mortar shell make a sound when it passes through the air?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, in this particular case, the one who hears the sound is lucky because -- they are lucky since the shrapnel continues on their way. But once it starts falling out of the sky, in that case, you don't hear it, you feel it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That, if it pleases you, Mr. President, Your Honours, concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Ms. Pilipovic, I see you are on your feet. You are going to cross-examine the witness? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before my friend proceeds, may I just clarify one thing? On the record we have -- it has been pointed out to me that in answer to a question I asked about the distance between the two impact sites, there is written here "45 metres, approximately." My memory is 4 to 5 metres. I don't know if perhaps I can ask him to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you ask for a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how far did this shell which impacted a few days after the incident of the 12th of July, 1993 fell in terms of the distance from the gate?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance was between 4 and 5 metres. 4 to 5, not 45. 4 to 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, you will now be examined by counsel for the Defence. Miss Pilipovic, please proceed. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. While Ms. Pilipovic will be examining the witness, could we have the original of the Prosecution's document, the medical certificate, in order to be able to examine it a little more clearly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, I see that you are already assisting the parties. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief with my learned colleague, you spoke about an incident that happened on the 12th of July, 1993. Could you tell us since when your sister has been living in that house and whether she is still living in that house now?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't talk about an incident. I would call it a massacre. But my sister moved into that house in the course of 1992, when the Serbs set fire to her house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who lived in the house in which your sister lived?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Munib Mujezinovic lives there, and in the course of the war, he moved to Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Up until when did your sister live in that house?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She didn't live in the house all the time. She moved into a flat towards the end of 1993. It was an abandoned flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that your sister in the course of 1992 and in 1993, that during that period she lived in that house?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She didn't live in that house in 1992. In 1992, in May, when the Serbs set fire to her house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you said that is when she moved into that house.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is when she came in that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That is what understood. So she lived in the house in the course of 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, when you went to your sister's, did you go there to visit her or did you go to collect water?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to collect water. I went there to give her something.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, could you tell us or could you confirm that on the 22nd of February, 1995, you gave a statement to the Bosnian authorities with regard to this incident?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement to the Bosnian authorities, but I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I say the Defence has a copy of the statement and the date is the 22nd of February, 1995, and that you have signed it, would you agree with this? Would that be the statement? I can show it to you if you like.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement in question. I know that it was in May [Real-time transcript read in error "February"] but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of February, 1995, when you gave the statement to the Bosnian authorities, did anyone with regard to the incident of the 12th of July, did anyone speak to you with regard to this incident?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere in respect of a matter of translation. I heard the English translation saying that, "I know it was in May, but I can't remember the exact date." It is in the transcript now that "I know that it was in February." I don't know whether this was a translation problem or in the next chain that is between the translation and the transcript. Was this a mistake? Of course, everyone makes mistakes. Was there a mistake in the translation or was it corrected in the transcript? Could perhaps the English booth --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said "May," as far as the interpreter can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then the translation was correct that it was May and it appears differently in the transcript. Could I just clarify this? Mr. Grebic, you said, when you were asked about the statement of which Ms. Pilipovic thought you did was the 22nd of February. In my transcript, I read that your answer was, "I know that it was -- " Well, I know that it is not the transcript. But I heard translated that you said, "I know that it was in May." Do you remember that it was in May or do you remember that it was in February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard to say exactly. That was a long time ago. Whether it was May or February, it is difficult to say. But it would sooner be February than May, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, your first question was, "The Defence has a copy of the statement on the 22nd of February," and the next question was, "On the 23rd of February, when you gave the statement." Which date is the correct one? I am just wondering whether there are two statements or --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I said the 23rd of February, 1995, because that is the only date I could have said since I have a statement with that date. I can't remember that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grebic. After that, did you give a statement to the investigators of the Prosecution on the 31 of August, 2000?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, when I asked you whether on the 12 of July, 1993, whether you went to visit your sister or you also went to collect water, you said you went to give her something?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To give her something, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the investigators of the Prosecution on the 30th of August, on the 31 of August, 2002, on the first page of that statement, of the translation, you said, On that day, I and a friend of mine went to get water. When I got there, I saw people there whom I knew." Could you tell us what is correct? Is what is correct that you went there on the 31 of August to get water or is what you are saying today correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am saying now is what is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why on the 31 of August, 2000, you said that you went to there to get water?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the investigators of the Prosecution, were you speaking in your own language?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement in its English version?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was -- did you listen to the dictation of the statement?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us how come in the record it says that you went to get water there with your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I said something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you admit that you may have perhaps gone there to collect water with your friend?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to collect water. I went to give something to my sister.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that what is stated in the statement that you have signed is not correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why with regard to this incident which you witnessed why you gave two different statements with regard to this incident?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the massacre, perhaps I said that I went to get water, but I didn't go to get water. I went to give something to my sister. In my opinion, that doesn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 12th of July, 1993, did you also go to see your sister?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How often would you go there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seldom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "seldom," could you be more precise? Was that once a week, once a month, or how often?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was seldom because I wasn't free to move. I was afraid of the shelling and of snipers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After the 12th of July, 1993, how often did you go to see your sister during the time she was living in that house?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to that place again until I took the investigators to that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you went to that place for the first time with the investigators?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that was on the 30th of -- the 31st of August, 2000?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you gave the statement, you said that you were with the investigators. After that, when you were leaving -- when you were going to the investigators, were you with them?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was with the investigators on two occasions. I was at the site of the massacre with the investigators on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you have confirmed that up until the 12th of July, you went there very seldom, and after the 12th of July, you didn't go there again, you didn't go to that street, to your sister's?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except when I took the investigators to show them that place, to show them where the massacre had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Grebic, on that day when you went there, my colleague asked you what the weather was like on that day. You said it was changeable, both cloudy and sunny.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, it was just before the rain so it was sunny and then it was cloudy.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did it rain on that day?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening and in the afternoon, too. It was just before the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you went there on that day on the 12th of July, 1993, you said that you didn't know what time it was; you said it was in the afternoon. Could you tell us whether the people in that street were standing or sitting?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were standing and some of them were sitting on the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many people there were in the line?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 20. Approximately, there were 20 and more than 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "20 or more than 20," do you mean to say that there may have been between 20 and 30?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count them but, in my opinion, it was perhaps 20, 25. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice or did you see, was there any soldiers waiting in that line?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you spoke to a woman who was in the queue. You said that her name was Dragica Micanovic. Could you tell us how old she was?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was about 55 and 60. She was between 55 and 60, in my opinion. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where she was standing when you spoke to her?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was standing outside the gate, two or three metres in front of the gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any people in front of her who were closer to the gate?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you entered the house or, rather, the yard, you said that you knocked on the door two or three times?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether there were people -- whether there were any people in the yard?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were perhaps three or four people in the yard around the well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the entrance to the house where you were standing, was there anyone standing by the door there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no one standing by the door, but to the right of the door, there was a group of young men between 16 and 17. They were playing cards. They were waiting in the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "a group of young men playing cards," how many of them were there and were they sitting or standing?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were sitting. There were some plastic tables, some old ones. There were three or four or five of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see whether there were any people by the well?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were, those whose turn it was and who would come to get the water.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When the incident occurred and when you told us that you had been wounded, can you confirm that at that time - and correct me if I am wrong - did you say that you stayed in the house for about ten minutes after you had felt that something was hurting you?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So after 15 or 20 minutes, you left the house. Can you tell us and can you describe what you saw in the yard?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When my sister helped me and her friend, I stayed there for a minute. They stopped the bleeding. I went to the hospital. I went out into the yard and I saw quite a few corpses and quite a few bodies and body parts. Those who were wounded, they tried to take them to the hospital, and the dead people remained lying there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- can you tell us how many people there were who were dead in the yard?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count, but about ten people. About ten bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you saw those ten bodies and the corpses?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say 10. I said about 10. Perhaps 10, perhaps 11. I apologise, perhaps 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see them in the yard?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them in the yard and some of them beyond the yard, outside the gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "outside the gate," can you be a little more precise? Can you tell us where they were with regard to the gate? Can you tell us where these bodies were and did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a street that ran alongside the gate, and I saw a woman on the pavement. I didn't know her. And in the middle of the street, I saw Mrs. Dragica Micanovic, and she was lying on her back and she was all black and swollen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the police came to the site?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not while I was there. Perhaps -- they probably came afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I have understood from your answer, there was -- you said there were two bodies lying in the street.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say two. There were more, but I noticed that woman on the pavement. I saw Dragica in the middle of the street and there were other bodies on the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the area you passed through, did you see any bodies? Did you see the consequences of the shell and did you see the leftover of the shell, parts of the shell, of the exploded shell?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about -- are you talking about the traces of the shell on the pavement?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you notice these traces, and did you see the tail of the shell?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That shell didn't leave any traces because it hit the body of a girl and that is when it exploded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you found out what the name of that girl was?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the name of that girl but I know that she died and her mother died, too. I later found out and I later met the father, Vlado Sana [phoen] quite by chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After those conversations, did you find out where that girl and her mother were standing?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Probably near the gate, but I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did that shell leave any traces on some other object? You said there were no traces on the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it left traces on the bodies and on the walls of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were those traces visible on the walls of the house and on which house?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the walls of the house in front of which water was being collected. And probably elsewhere too, but I didn't notice this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "the house in which they were collecting water," does that mean the house in which your sister was living?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, on the outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you very well when you said on the walls.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the walls on the outside, the traces of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did the traces of the shell face the street?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After you left the hospital, did you find out whether the police went to the site of the massacre? Was that site recorded and did UNPROFOR go there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about it. I heard that the police went there and that UNPROFOR went there, too, and I know that they filmed that site. I heard that this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you heard that the police went there, could you tell us whether do you know how long after the incident the police went there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was in the hospital at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you stayed in your sister's house for 15 to 20 minutes, 15 to 20 minutes. All the bodies of all the people who had died on that occasion, were they there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who died remained there. Only those who were wounded were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there were any cars on that street?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was probably one car there in front of the gate, on the left-hand side, but I can't remember the make of the car and I can't remember its colour either.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were a member of the BH army from April 1993?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which military formation you belonged to in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I belonged to the so-called Dobrinja Brigade, the 105th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the Dobrinja Brigade," which was later the 105th Brigade, is that is brigade whose commander was Ismet Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which military formation, which other military formation with regard to the brigade that you belonged to, was it a battalion, a company?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I belonged to the 3rd Battalion of a company.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the command post of your company was and of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was somewhere within Dobrinja, away from the site of the massacre, a bit further up. And the command post of my company was in the Lav Tolstoj Street on the opposite side of the school. I can't remember the name of the school. It was facing Lukavica and the church.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, if we show you a map of Sarajevo, a map of Dobrinja, would you be able to pinpoint the location of the company's command post and the command post of the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, we have a map of the town. We have prepared a map. I apologise, I haven't inscribed the number. 95, I think. We haven't solved the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, could you please assist Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the witness the map in colour and put it on the ELMO in order to orientate himself better.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, on your right side, there is a map of the town. It might be easier if you have a look at the map itself. It is to your right. Could you just put the map a bit further up so that Dobrinja might be more visible. Please put it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could you please help the witness, please. Just a bit further up. You can see where Dobrinja. We all need to see it. That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you also please adjust the microphone of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command of the staff was in the Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, could you please take a pencil and mark number 1 at the point which you call the command of the staff? Please take a black felt tip and mark number 1 at the site that you call -- but use a fine-tipped felt tip in order to avoid problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please provide the fine-tip pen to the witness in black. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, you have just marked a number 1 there. Could you please repeat which command post was there, was it the staff command of the brigade or of the Battalion?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's the street?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the boulevard of Dobrinja. The command post of the brigade has been marked as number one in the street of Branilaca Dobrinja. Could you indicate the command post of your 3rd Battalion on the map.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is -- I don't know what this street was called afterwards. It was Lav Tolstoj Street. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, is that the street of Emile Zola? Are you telling us that that's where the command post for the 3rd Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the street to the right in the direction of Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark by number 2, notwithstanding you can't tell where the Emile Zola Street -- ?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see Emile Zola Street but I don't see the street where my command post was for the third company.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the battalion?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the street from Emile Zola. I don't know the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark by number 2 next to the Emile Zola Street and then for the record we will consider what you are saying. If you could just put number 2 next to the Emile Zola Street.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the witness marked by number 2, the location of or rather the command post of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell us where the command post for your company was?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, where I marked it by number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the battalion?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same street of the Boulevard Branilaca Dobrinja. I can't remember the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So could we correct the record, if you can place number 3 where the command post for your battalion was situated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, number 3 marks the command post for the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, for the marking on the map, it's not necessary for the transcript to repeat it, it's only when the witness points at the place, which leaves no traces. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, you are saying that the command post for your company was in the vicinity of Emile Zola Street and you marked it by number 2. Are you telling us that is where the front line was where you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front line was in the direction of Lukavica and the direction of the church perhaps 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you use the marker and indicate the direction?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can place an arrow in the direction of Lukavica Road. I can't really mark it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us about the buildings where the command posts were situated both for the chief of staff and the brigade, the battalion and the company, what were those buildings?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were residential buildings and they were then turned into office buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you identify what buildings they were and what they were called, where the command post for your company, your Battalion was, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact name of the street but I know there used to be a UPI supermarket there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that the command post of your company was in the building where the supermarket was?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There used to be a supermarket there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did that residential building also include flats?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The part of the building in the direction on the -- of the Lukavica was shelled and part of the building had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to your command post, the command post of your company and the building where it was situated, could you tell us how far away it was from the positions of the Republika Srpska Army in relation to that part of town, Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My front line -- my line was in front of the church. The part of my battalion and my company, about 500 metres away, and the Serb forces were in front of us in the church by 300 metres away, in Dobrinja IV and Dobrinja I to the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: For all intents and purposes, could you just mark the positions or rather the location of the church and Dobrinja I on the map, if you can.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the church being marked here or even the school. So it is a bit difficult to find my way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the name of the school was?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure. But I think it was Dusan Pajic or something along these lines before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was this school open during the war?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it was on the line, on the front line. It was the demarcation line so it wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that in the church -- in the school, sorry, as you call it, Dusan Pajic, there was soldiers there and it was the front line?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- I am referring to 1993, 1994, you said you were in the army of 1993 -- were there any changes to these front lines, or demarcation lines?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I joined the BH army, I was living in town, near Hepok. In 1993, the beginning of June 1993, I went back to Dobrinja with my family, and those lines were not changed. I found them in that way and I was on duty there, I was a guard there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I remind you that the Defence took the same time as the Prosecution did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try and wrap this up before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, could you tell us about this period of time when it comes to the two armed forces in the area of Dobrinja, were there any battles there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and there were no movements of units. We were simply on guard duty. And the Serb snipers used to shoot the civilians and in the direction of our settlements.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any snipers within your company?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we did not have any snipers in the BH army. At least not in that area where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a company called Cenex? Are there premises of that company near Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the 1st Motorised Brigade being near Stup?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was stationed there, I don't know what brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what weapons you had?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a machine-gun. I had a gun, sorry. It was a Kalasnikov type gun made in Yugoslavia in Kragenjevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said you had a Kalasnikov. The other people, how were they dressed, the other members of your --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had semi-automatic guns and Kalasnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your uniform was like? Did you have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have any uniforms. Those who had money had uniforms and they had them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how much time you spent on the front line and where did you have your meals?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The food was delivered to the front line where we were stationed. I was on guard duty for two days at a time, or rather once every six or eight hours for two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you were there for two days, where did you go to sleep?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In abandoned buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: These abandoned buildings in Dobrinja, were they residential buildings? Were they being used for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were residential buildings, but we used to go and sleep in the cellars

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us and do you know anything about where the members of the brigade would gather in case it was necessary for them to group together? Did you have a place in Dobrinja such as a barracks or something?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any barracks, and my company used to gather in a garage. It was near the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us in what building the command post of your battalion was situated?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command post was situate in the boulevard of Branilaca, Dobrinja, where they used to be a furniture shop called Jugodrvo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were the premises of Jugodrvo where this particular building, were there any residential buildings in the area, in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were right above the battalion premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the 105th Brigade, where was that situated, the command post, I mean?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The street was called Dobrinjka Bolnica [phoen], if I remember correctly, and on the other side was Bulevar Branilaca, and the command post was in the offices of Magros.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grebic, you said that you spent between five and six days at the hospital. You said that afterwards you went back to hospital for treatment. On those occasions, did the doctors record any of the dates of the visits and the treatment?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you got this letter of discharge?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in the 17th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you got that letter when you left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that -- well, during the examination in chief, you said that there were other incidents, or shelling incidents, and you said that there were something about five or six days after the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of making a statement, you never mentioned this incident whereby your sister was injured?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, she was not badly injured, but it skinned the surface of her head so it took away some of her hair.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the direction from which the shell came?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't fire it, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this incident on the 12th of July, when you yourself were wounded? Do you know anything about the positions where the shell could have been fired from?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is up to the experts to determine that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us from what positions and from what places you can get the best view of the street where people were queueing up for water? Can you actually see the buildings around it?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have seen very well from Gavrica, which was in the hand of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You did mention this hill Gavrica Brdo in your statement. Can you show us where exactly it is?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, if you have the relevant map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it on the map in front of you? What part of town is the Gavrica Brdo?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the part of town which is above Gornji Kotorac. I don't seem to be able to find Gornji Kotorac. Gornji Kotorac is a bit lower down. No, it is Gornji Kotorac I am talking about. You can't see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the direction in relation to the place where the incident took place, the general direction that you say marked the place that had a good view of the area? From -- in what direction is it? If you could just indicate it.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not an expert on maps. I just can't see it here. I can tell you what my assumption would be. I said that it was in the direction of this Gavrica Brdo. I thought that was the place where you could have the best view of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark the place where the incident took place? According to your opinion, where is the street where the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The street is not marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what is the name of the street? Was it the street of Spasenija Cana Babovic or some other street?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, it is before you reach the top of the hill. It was called Aleja Branka Bujic, and it was where just a couple of private houses were situated. And then when the settlements went up, the name was changed and it was then called Spasenija Cana Babovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the current name of the street?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the street now, it was named after Hakije Turajlica, who was the Vice President of the government and was killed by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this street Spasenija Cana Babovic, could you tell us how far the front line was?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the house, as I said, in the direction of Nedzarici, about 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You did say that the tunnel was being built at that time. Could you -- I mean, in your statement, you said that that place was about -- the entry into the tunnel was about 100 metres away. Could you tell us whether the armed forces were organising the security in the area whilst the tunnel was being built?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not the armed forces. It was the Civil Defence and the private citizens, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Stamp, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you had a Kalasnikov while you were on gourd duty near to the demarcation line. Did you carry home that weapon?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't carry it home because we didn't have enough weapons, so I used to leave it to the next person who came on duty when I was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said your company congregated in a garage near the demarcation line and that you also slept in cellars of abandoned residential building. How far or how close were these abandoned buildings to the demarcation line?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said between 500 and 600 metres in some areas, and in other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. areas they were closer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you were on duty and you slept in abandoned residential buildings, can you say where these abandoned residential buildings were in respect to the demarcation line?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The particular building where I used to go whilst I was on duty, where I used to go to rest between rounds of duty whilst I was working, was in Lav Tolstoj Street , which is in the direction of Lukavica and Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Civil Defence personnel and the civilians who organised the security around the area where the tunnel was being constructed, were they armed or not?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but those who had arms, perhaps rifles or guns from earlier on, probably yes. They might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Grebic, I have just a few short questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether the tunnel you talk about, was dug from both sides of the airport or from one side to the other, and then in which direction?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tunnel was being dug from the direction of Butmir and from the direction of Dobrinja, and it was going below the runways of the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question is: You told us that the woman to whom you talked before the shell fell on the 12th of July, that she was living in the airport facility which was held by the Serb forces. Would that mean that she was still living there or that she used to live there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the aggression, she used to live in the so-called airport settlement and when the Serb force withdrew and when they -- when the UNPROFOR forces took over the airport, some of the civilians left, some of them wanted to move within Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And she stayed there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She left her apartment and remained in Dobrinja to live, where the other citizens were living. She went through all this horror in much the same way as everybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a last question or perhaps two questions in respect of your discharge letter. Could perhaps the discharge letter be shown again to the witness. That is P151. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wouldn't like to interrupt you, but whilst you are showing the letter, could we just remind the witness once again that it is not a custom here to use the term "aggression," as we can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... testimony. Mr. Grebic, could you look at the document, and there seems to be some shadowy parts where there might have been something. Do you see that? It seems to be at the right in the middle, some shadowy signs or might have been text or... Do you remember whether there was any such thing on the letter you received or was it just the text as you can read it on this letter?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether there was anything or not. But I would just like to tell you that at that time we didn't have the technology for clean and nice printing. We didn't even have adequate paper and we used to have to print on paper which had already been used for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my last question to you: You told us that you received this letter and that your name was put on it by hand, correcting a wrong first letter. Did you happen to keep that letter?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be willing to provide the letter to the Court?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I must still have it at home, but I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But would you be willing to try to find it and to give it to an official of the Court or of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN GREBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I manage to do it, I would be pleased to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this answer. Mr. Grebic, you have answered all the questions put to you by both the Prosecution and the Defence and the additional questions of the Chamber. It is very important for this Chamber to hear the testimony of those who have been present during the relevant times at relevant places. It will assist us in performing our task. Since we also know that it is quite a journey for you to come from Sarajevo to The Hague, we would like to thank you very much for coming and I hope you have a safe journey home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp, is this anything we should deal with in the presence of the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think it really matters much. There had been a document yesterday which the Court had indicated that it would prefer if it came into evidence the document. We have laminated copies which we have taken from the binder for the witness that we intended to tender them through. They're marked P1386, and the translation P1386.1. I think shortly before we started, my learned friend Ms. Pilipovic were given -- was given a copy, and I don't know if she would object, but we could tender these to the Court and perhaps it could be agreed that they are received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I think it was the Defence who wanted to tender the documents, but you had no copies for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The Defence didn't intend to tender this on our behalf and that is why we made that statement yesterday

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, you know that the Court, since a lot of questions have been put in respect of the that document, that the Court would like to have the documents referred to in evidence. So, we can do a few things. One of the things is to wait for the Prosecution; the other thing would be that we order the parties to put into evidence these documents; and the third option would be that you make up your mind on whether you still do not want to tender the document into evidence. Let me just hear. You are still of the same position that you don't want to tender the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document was presented to the witness, the witness answered questions about this document. The witness did say that the photographs are true representations of the scene of the incident that we are speaking about just now and the Prosecution tenders this document and asks that it be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The formal obstacle might be that the Prosecution did not introduce the document by the witness, but I think the Chamber also decided that we want to have it in evidence. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. First let me given an opportunity to Mr. Stamp to finish what he wanted to say because I interrupted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think though the formal practice is that the party who first hands the witness a document is the party who tenders it, however, I think it is sufficient if the witness identifies the document as being relevant to the case and, if so, that is something that we are entitled to tender. May it please you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, thank you for giving me this opportunity to reply. The Defence would not object to having the Prosecution tendering this document. That would be the clearest option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not even if it was done immediately now at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, Mr. President, it doesn't matter when this is done. We agree on the principle, whenever this takes place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I take it then that the document is tendered by the Prosecution at this moment and -- is there any objection against the admission into evidence because that is a different question whether you tender it or have an objection to the admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not at all. We have no objection to this other issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is then admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, we are at a moment where we usually have a break. Perhaps we could deal with the documents after the break. And I would also like to take the opportunity then to see whether there are any remaining problems in respect of the documents attached to the expert report the Prosecution is intending to tender, the export report of Mr. Donia. So if you would please prepare for that so that we can discuss it, but let's do it efficiently. We will then have a break until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 4.23 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I assume that I said we would have a break until 10 minutes past 4.00 but at the same time, when I left this courtroom, I recognised that it was a violation of the customary law that the first break would be half an hour. I now see in the transcript it says that we have until 20 minutes past 4.00. But let's forget about it. Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents in relation to the witness Grebic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1517B, discharge certificate in B/C/S; Exhibit P1517B.1, English translation; Exhibit D95, map marked by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I perhaps ask Mr. Stamp whether you would be able to, in one way or the other, to make sure that the translation on which Mr. Piletta-Zanin has studied already would be a final translation. I mean, draft always gives the impression that it is not properly done or... But before asking you, perhaps I should ask whether Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as I invited him to do, to ask whether there are any specific problems, not general but specific problems bothering him in relation to the legible text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I have certain difficulties, not with regard to the legibility of the text, but with regard to the fact that it just can't be read, that is to say that the text that is present seems to be legible, it seems to have been translated in a fairly orderly manner, but, however, there are certain elements which are illegible, and this might be of importance. And this is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please first answer my question. My question was whether those parts legible, whether the translation caused you any specific concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yes and the -- I said no, and the translation seems to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then next question: Are there any other objections against --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. There are other objections which I have presented, and I apologise for this. It is a matter of taking into consideration the fact that part of the text which appears in some of the photocopies, the ones that we have, part of this text can't be found in the documents that were provided by the Prosecution and aren't originals. So yet again, we have casting doubt on the authentic character of these documents and we request that the Prosecution gives us, once and for all, for all these medical documents, that the Prosecution provides us with the originals so that we can have a clear view of them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let me just make one observation in this respect. The Defence is as such not entitled to ask for originals, but of course, and that is the way I understand your objection, they can object against the admissibility of documents because the Defence takes the position that, without having seen the originals, they cannot check whether it is a copy of an original or, as you expressed several times, it is manipulated or changed, or whatever way, a different document. So when you are asking the Prosecution to produce originals, they have just one obligation and that is to provide you with the copies of the documents you have. But I do understand your objection in this way that you say, we object because it is not an original, which is not the same as that the Prosecution should provide you with originals. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. We have to decide on the documents presented to us. Let me just confer with my colleagues. Is there any response you would like to make, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. We have heard the testimony as far as the handwritten part is concerned. We have heard the testimony as far as the content of the document is concerned. We also have heard the testimony of the witness, a possible explanation for those parts of the document are just shadowy there. The witness testified that under the circumstances at that time one was forced to use several times paper that had been used before. Having given the decisions in this respect and adding to it that the Chamber will, of course, have to assess the probative value of the document, we still had a problem in respect of the attachments to the report of Mr. Donia. I asked the parties. We have seen the correspondence on it. May I first just ask the Prosecution how the Prosecution intends to deal with the attachments to the report of Mr. Donia. I don't know if it is you or Mr. Ierace, Mr. Stamp, that deals with it. If it is Mr. Ierace, then I would rather do it when he is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, there is no translation, unfortunately, and my colleague doesn't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...until the interpretation is functioning again. I will just go on speaking slowly until I get a sign that the translation is in place again. Yes, I got the sign. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I understand the problem correctly, the Defence would like to have copies of what we designate as open source materials, material coming from documents published in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what way the report of the expert refers to these public domain sources, just by referring or did he attach it to his -- ?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just by reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just by reference. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Defence has asked for them, and while we are of the view that in respect to open source material we are not obliged to give them copies, we have delivered to them those that we can immediately lay our hands on and we are undertaking to provide the remainder as quickly as possible just to expedite proceedings and for the convenience of my friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that the Prosecution, those open source documents the expert is referring to and has not attached to his report, that those open source documents have been provided to the Defence when they were in the possession and could be easily traced by the Prosecution and that you will further assist the Defence in obtaining copies, if you find them, and you are trying to do your best.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. I would not be in a position to say to what extent some of these documents have previously been given to the Defence. However, we delivered nine to them yesterday, I think, and we will give them the rest as soon as possible. And I am referring to whatever documents which are published within the public domain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That is one issue. There was another issue about two pages that have been provided to the Defence by now. If I am well informed, it was your letter of -- let me just turn -- but there were two specific pages that the Defence asked for and they have been provided as well, as far as I understand. That was page -- let me just have a look. Page 3200 and 3199. I take it from your letter of the 12th of April that they have been provided to the Defence. I am referring to the letter of Mr. Ierace of the 12th of April 2002, when he says, "During the break you also mentioned that you are missing pages of 3200 and 3199. We are providing you copies of these pages and will place them in your locker today." So may I take it that you found them, first of all?
