utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if the Prosecution says that that is the case and if we haven't found it yet, we will find it. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...the other problem about pages 3233 through 3199, so it should be 34 pages of which we had some difficulties in tracing them so as to understand them. Is that part of the problem solved as well? Those pages of which the Prosecution writes to the Defence in the letter of the 12th of April, "During a break you explained that you mean by these number certain pages of the report which are identified by the Registry's pagination and which contained citations or quotes taken from material." Does that still cause any problem or is there no problem in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I found it difficult to follow you, I have to admit. Are we sure that we are speaking of these pages or have you found the reference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The letter of the 12th of April, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Mr. Ierace. I will try to find it. I will try to find it and to see about that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there were three letters on the 10th of April. Let me ask you differently. Is there any remaining problem - that's what interests me most, as a matter of fact - in regard of the document? Not the public source documents, but the other documents related to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think that there are other problems. We received under certain -- number certain documents. These documents don't correspond to this designation, to this number. And I pointed out to my learned colleague yesterday evening, I pointed out which documents were in question and I think that we were able to conclude that the documents that we had under this number weren't the ones that the Prosecution should have provided us with. So I don't think that I have received any news about this from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you understand French, could you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, are the pages 3033 up until 3389 concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That could be the case but I will have a look because we have two different figures, but I will see about that. But Prosecution knows because this matter was mentioned during the break. Mr. President, there is a problem which persists and it relates to a cassette. We think that there is a cassette with regard to the intervention made by Mr. Cavic. This cassette was mentioned in a note, a note in page 20, on page 20 of Mr. Donia's report, or certain elements which were quoted in this report, and we think that this interview is absolutely essential in order to be able to see exactly what might have been said or decided in this cassette. So if this cassette was produced, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please indicate to me Page 20's footnotes, which footnote --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, we are talking about -- no, it is translation error. It is a note, note 20, and this document by the historian, Robert Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Footnote 20 on page 17, speech by Radovan Karadzic to the Serb people, November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. That is exact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there are ERN numbers. Would that mean that this video is in the possession of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't know. We may have it. I will make enquiries as to whether we do, and if we do, then I will provide a copy to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Donia relies on a transcript rather than a tape. So although it is not strictly required, if we have it, we will provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps the ERN numbers refers to transcripts because I see that it is in two different languages. And since I never noticed any voiceovers, that I assume that it relates to the transcript of the video, at least, and then we can read the text. Are there any other problems in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The document which we were referring to -- which we are referring to, concerns a number, P1262. These are documents which have the ERN number R00460916 and the following. But these documents seem to have been introduced, inserted under a number whereas they should not have been. In other words, these documents are perfectly legible, but it seems to us that they have been lost under this number and that there are other documents which we should have found them. It is probably a technical error. Mr. President, yesterday evening, we briefly met with my learned colleagues who are in front of me. I showed it in my dossier; I told them about my problem. And that is the stage we are at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you think the solution could be found for the problem raised yesterday during your meeting with Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that the problem that he first referred to, that my learned colleague first referred to, may be dealt with by the matter of sorting the document that he has. So perhaps at the next break, he could speak to my case manager. We might be able to overcome that problem. Excuse me, Mr. President. Yes, I think that covers that last concern expressed by Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Might I raise two issues in relation to Mr. Donia as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The first is, I would like to inform you of the course I propose to take in examination-in-chief with Mr. Donia, which is simply to qualify him and then to have him identify his report, and nothing more. In other words, if I take that course, examination in chief should be over in a matter of minutes. I propose to take that course because his report is relatively brief. I don't think it needs any amplification or expansion. This seems to me the most sensible approach. I mention it at this stage firstly so as to invite Your Honours to read the report before he gives his evidence, and secondly, if there would be any objection in relation to that approach or concern from the Bench, that we do amplify it. Then, of course, in relation to the latter concern, I would do it. Mr. President, the second issue is in relation to the material referred to in the footnotes. I take the view that it is not only not necessary but would, in the circumstances, be efficient to not tender that material. If, however, Your Honours would prefer that we did tender it, then we would be happy to do so. So I would be grateful for any indication at this stage or guidance in that respect. Finally, Mr. Donia is able to give evidence from Thursday until and including Monday, being three days. I don't suggest by saying that that three days of cross-examination would be appropriate or anything like that. I simply wish to make clear to Your Honours the period of time that he is available. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, the Chamber is confronted with a situation that when we read the report, we might want to read the footnotes and the material contained in it as well. If ever we would want to rely on these sources, they have to be properly introduced into the trial. That means that the Prosecutor should prepare for tendering the supporting materials as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. One of the problems, one of the reasons for which we asked for all these documents, is that we know that Mr. Donia's report is not what we would call in historian's terms, a primary report. It is a secondary report. That is to say, this person was not relying on the information that he may have obtained himself. So it concerns specific -- it didn't concern specific research in archives but he based himself exclusively on the work Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or on -- on the work of third parties. So we are on the secondary domain. Without these documents, obviously, we won't be able to see the matter very clearly, all the more so that 80 per cent of these supporting documents, another team made these calculations. Eighty per cent of these documents are documents, the origin of which is partly -- it comes from one side and not from another side. These documents originate from one side, and this is why the Defence is being very careful with such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have listened carefully to this observation. Then the last question in relation to Mr. Donia was, until now, the Defence has not given an indication on how much time they would need to cross-examine Mr. Donia. When we asked it before, we heard some objections in relation to documents not yet being provided to the Defence. We now have a better idea of what portion that is, which is a smaller portion, a relatively small portion. Would the Defence please indicate how much time they think they would use for cross-examination of Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. I suppose, well, don't shoot the messenger. This is a very bad piece of news I am giving you. We are talking about two days of cross-examination. It may be rather exceptional in the light of what the Prosecution has said, but we do have implications there which are probably easy to understand for all of us. Mr. Donia has worked a great deal on contemporary history. He talked about and worked on Austro-Hungary. He is a person who is likely to be able to provide us with extremely information with reference to this entire problem, not just with reference to General Galic or what he might be accused of but all the related issues as well. We all do know that this is a very complex issue we are talking about and therefore we must spend the necessary amount of time on that, and we will probably have to trace all this back to the time in the past in order to be able to get a global and overall view within a historic context of what was likely to happen. And this sort of information is absolutely indispensable in the mind of the Defence. Apart from that, I myself unfortunately are going to be absent on Friday. I very much regret that. I would like to point it out immediately. So that this cross-examination will have to take part in two parts. First of all, I, myself, would like to cross-examine the witness and then Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...given us the reasons why you would need them. Having dealt with the Donia report -- Mr. Ierace, you are nodding no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I have just been handed by the court usher a letter in the elegant French language from my learned colleague which, with my rudimentary understanding of French, I perceive to relate to Mr. Donia. It seems therefore there are some outstanding issues but I can't inform the Trial Chamber what they are. I will take some steps to have the letter translated as quickly as possible

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would please try to learn French, Mr. Ierace, by the next break. I think it is time whether the Prosecution is ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you'll excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stamp, it is you who are going to examine the next witness. Mr. Usher, could you please lead in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we proceed with that, Mr. President, I don't know if the Court formally received the evidence P1386 and the translation thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1386. Yes, I think when it was tendered, that we said that it was admitted. Well, we asked for it ourselves. Now we also received a copy with the photographs in P1386 and the copies of the photographs in the translation in P1386.1. Mr. Stamp, then we will wait until the witness has arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mehonic, I presume. Mr. Mehonic, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. And the text of this solemn declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher, and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you start by telling us your name?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: My name is Rasim Mehonic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where do you live, Mr. Mehonic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: At the moment, in Sarajevo in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Since 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you work now, Mr. Mehonic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, I am a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you recall the years of 1992, 1993, and 1994, were you working then? Were you employed then?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you a pensioner then?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In what part of Sarajevo did you live in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in what part of Dobrinja did you live at?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja II.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall the 12th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- start by telling us about the weather that day, what was it like?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: It was sunny up until between 3.00 and 4.00, and after the tragedy, it started to rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the tragedy that you mentioned, where did this happen?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: In Dobrinja, this is called Kvadrant C, at the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And about what time did this tragedy occur?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Either at ten to 4.00 or ten after 4.00 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us what time you arriveD there before this tragedy occurred?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I got there at around 10.00, together with my wife, who died, and I had two daughters who had already been there earlier. And they died as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your daughters had gone there to collect drinking water; is that so?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And they would have to line up to wait to get to the pump; is that so?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say about what time your daughters went to join the line?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: At around 2.00 a.m., so that they could get to the pump in good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After yourself and your wife joined them, which was at about 10.00 in the morning, for how long did you remain together?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: We stayed together up until ten to 4.00 or ten past 4.00. I can't remember exactly. At around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now at the time the tragedy occurred, where had you all reached in the line going to the pump?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I was the second in line. Just one more family was going to collect water and then it was our turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you know Enver Taslaman?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was crouching next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were you crouching? Where was this that you were crouching at next to him?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: In the courtyard where the well and the pump were situated. Next to the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were you doing there next to him?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Well, I had back pain and I couldn't stand and so I was hoping that there would be somewhere to sit, but he didn't have somewhere to sit and that is why he was crouching and I was crouching next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where were your wife and daughters at this time?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: They were out in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see other people there at about that time?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw other people who were waiting in line, elderly people, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you say, "a tragedy occurred," can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that a shell landed and killed 12 people and wounded 14 and I, myself, was wounded as well. And that is why I call it a tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When this shell landed, did you see or hear anything?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I just heard the explosion since I was in the courtyard. I heard the explosion. I tried to get out and check on my family. I was stepping over dead and wounded bodies. I managed to get out and I saw that they were all dead, and then I fainted as well and I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you step out through the gate into the road?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did you see outside the gate?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: What else could I see but 12 dead bodies and 14 or 15 wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where was your family at the time, your wife and daughters?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: They were lying dead in the street, one closer to the railing next to the gate, and my daughters were out in the street lying there dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you fainted. Were you taken anywhere after that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes. Somebody picked me up, I don't know who it was, and they took me to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you suffer any injuries and, if so, can you just tell us about them, please.

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes. The entire left side of my body was covered in wounds, and I still have a piece of shrapnel in my lung. It is lodged in my lung.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And which hospital did you go to?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: The Dobrinja Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say how long you remained at Dobrinja Hospital?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: 24 hours. Then I was taken to Kosevo Hospital, to the pulmonary unit, where I had surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say why you were taken -- well, you were taken to the Kosevo Hospital for surgery. Where did you travel to get to Kosevo Hospital from Dobrinja? Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was conscious at that stage. We went down the main road, although it was close to traffic. When we drove by, a sniper shot at us and I asked the driver, "Why are you talking this road?" And he replied: "Well, it is a matter of life and death for you."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You recall what vehicle you travelled in to go to Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that clearly. It was a Golf Volkswagen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was anybody in the car, do you know, dressed in military uniform or had weapons?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, no. Nobody else. I was alone with the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many times was the car shot at?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember the route that you took to Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes. From Dobrinja to Nedzarici, because there was no other possibility. And then we drove down another road; I can't remember what the name of the street is, it has been changed, in the direction of Marinevoj [phoen], and then from Marinevoj in the direction of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you say that when you drove by to get to Kosevo Hospital, a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sniper shot at you or shot at the vehicle that you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apparently no, but the interpreters haven't heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mehonic, all your answers are translated to us because we do not understand your language. We see you nodding, but the interpreters who are sitting behind you cannot see the expression of your face. So would you please answer by speaking words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. I must make an objection here, Mr. President, because I get the impression that the witness has already replied to the questions as to how many times they were shot at and he said "none."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the objection is denied because he always testified that he was sniped at. So there is a contradiction at this moment in his answers and, therefore, the objection is denied. Mr. Stamp is entitled to have the issue clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Between 8 and 10 days. I can't remember. And I wasn't actually cured. I still had a shunt and the blood was being drained out of my lungs and the lining of the lungs, and it is just that the hospital was full and they had no spare beds so I was sent home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you still have a piece of shrapnel in your left lung. Do you suffer any --

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- other long-term physical disability from your injuries that day?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't lie on my left side at all. Probably I have a problem because of that injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your wife and daughters, two daughters died. Were they buried?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Not on that day. Because we couldn't even have them -- have a burial before the night fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you attend that funeral?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before the incident of the 12th of July, 1993, was there shelling and sniping in that part of Dobrinja where you lived at?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreters didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was sniping and shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say where the sniping came from?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could say approximately from Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the shelling, can you say where the shelling came from?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell exactly where from. There were two places where shells used to come from, Gavrica Brdo and Sumarska Skola in Alija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you were discharged from the Kosevo Hospital, did you receive a medical document?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, a letter of discharge which I enclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you bring that letter of discharge to The Hague when you travelled here?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I submitted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, with your leave, may I tender to the witness Exhibit P1517C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And to the Court, that document as well as P1517C.1, which is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that document that you have there a copy of the medical release papers that you brought with you to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned an area, Gavrica Brdo. Can you say which party to the conflict controlled that area? Was it the Bosnian Serb army or was it the army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb army. Both of these locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, where did you live? Can you remember what type of building you lived in, in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: It was a six-storey building. I can't remember how long the building was. It had four entrances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it occupied or used by the military?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No. They were flats, private plats there. People lived in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this building ever shelled?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say in 1993 and 1994, going up to August, approximately how many times that building was hit by shells?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Seven times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, very much, Mr. President. That concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Before giving an opportunity to the Defence to put questions to you, Mr. Mehonic, do you still have the document in front of you, P1517? Or Mr. Usher, could you please put it in front of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As you might see in the left part of it, approximately the fifth line, it says, as far as I can read: "PIO, BIH Sarajevo." That is the line where the first word reads - I am certainly pronouncing it wrongly - " Radno" and "Osiguranje." Could you tell us what "PIO" stands for?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mehonic, good day.

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that on the 23rd of February, 1993, you made a statement in the Ministry of the Interior, the security services centre in Sarajevo, with regards to the incident that happened on the 12th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The statement that you gave on that occasion, did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From the time of that incident in which, as you said, you lost two daughters and a wife and you were wounded, from that moment onwards, did someone from the authorities, from the government or from the BH army, speak to you about that incident?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So the first time was on the 23rd of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm whether in that same year, in February, you gave a statement to the investigators for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: In the same year, yes, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, you said that you were in Kvadrant C in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which street that is, what the name of the street was?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't interested in going around there unless it was necessary to go there to collect water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is not an objection, it is a request for clarification. Perhaps if my friend -- this is we could do in re-examination, but I see here a couple of questions here being asked about a statement being made on the 23rd of February, 1993 in respect of an incident that occurred on the 12th of July in the same year. That is what I have in my record, the 23rd of February. I don't know if my friend wants to clarify that or if you could save it for later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, could you clarify the issue? It reads on the transcript, on page 61, line 9, your question was: "So the first time was on the 23rd of February, 1993." I am sure that was a mistake. Where the mistake was made doesn't interest me that much. What year did you have in mind while putting the question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I asked the witness the question, I was talking about the statement of the 23rd of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clarififies the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness said that in 1995, on the 23rd of February, he gave a statement for the first time to the authorities of the ministry of the government of the Bosnia and Herzegovina with regards to the incident that took place on the 12th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mehonic, you said that in that same year you spoke to and gave a statement to the investigators for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that but I don't remember the exact date, whether it was in the same year, around the new year, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mehonic. My last question before we spoke about this problem was: Do you know what the name of the street was in Kvadrant C?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how far you were -- how far your flat was from the place you went to to collect water?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 12th of July, 1993, did you go to collect water? Did you go to that street to collect water?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that day on the 12th of July, when you went there, you said that you arrived at about 10.00 in the morning. Could you tell us how many people there were in the street?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact number, but about 100. There were about 100 canisters, about 100 containers of water, so there must have been the same number of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there were about 100 canisters, is it on the basis of the number of canisters that you have come to the conclusion that there were 100 people or were there actually 100 people?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I concluded on the basis of the canisters because I couldn't see the people as they were hiding under the stairway and I couldn't count the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that in the street where you saw the canisters, you weren't able to see the people; the people weren't lining up in a traditional line?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: How could they line up as there were snipers shooting and they wouldn't let anyone in peace? Would you stand there and let someone shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mehonic, the street in which you were waiting in line, you and your family, to collect water, how far was the sniper from that street? Could you indicate the positions?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. I don't know anything about that. I wasn't a soldier and I wasn't involved in that. I only know that shots were fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mehonic, with regard to the place where the incident took place, do you know how far the confrontation lines were from that site?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, I never measured this neither in metres or kilometre. I don't know anything about this. The army knows about this. I wasn't a soldier. This is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible, given the street and the buildings in that street, in your opinion, was it possible to see that place from the position held by the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: From Gavrica Brdo, yes, it was possible to see it from that position, but from Nedzarici, no, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how far Gavrica Brdo is from the place where you were waiting in line for water?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I can give you a precise answer, but about 2 kilometres, or maybe a kilometre and a half or something like that. Because it is elevated, it is possible to have a good view of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mehonic, you have told us that you don't know how far the front lines were from the place where you were waiting for water.

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I am going to show you part of your statement which you gave to the investigators for the Prosecution on the 12th of November, 1995 -- the 20th of November. That is document 009 -- 008131 is the translation. It Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is the second page of the document. You said, "In the meantime the Bosnian army had advanced in that area and part of the conflict moved over towards Nedzarici."

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: "On the other side, it was protected by the presence of UNPROFOR at the airport?"

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: "But at that time the confrontation line was very near. It was about 50 metres away."

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: You have asked me a question about where the crime took place, and that was further from there. But where we went to collect water, that is quite correct, I gave that, I said that, but that wasn't 50 to 100 metres away. There was no water there then. The water supply had been cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that there was another place for water?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: There were several places because the entire settlement could not have collected water just from one place. People went wherever they could get water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I ask you, you cited the witness where in his written statement he says, "In the meantime the Bosnian army had advanced in that area." Could you inform the Court what "in the meantime," means. It seems that it does not relate to a specific moment. Could you please clarify for us what we have to understand by "in the meantime." Or ask the witness, or I don't know what he was referring to "in the meantime," but it is not a single moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. The witness spoke about the place where people went to collect water. Before saying "in the meantime," before the word "in the meantime," I will read out what the witness stated. I just wanted to be brief. "Before this incident, no one was killed or wounded in the immediate vicinity of that site. At that time, the place could be seen very well from the Serbian positions. In the meantime, the Bosnian army made progress." I am going to ask the witness what time he was thinking of when he spoke about the progress made by the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILOPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mehonic, when you said in your statement that "in the meantime the Bosnian army had made progress," could you tell us what period you were referring to? Was it before the incident of the 12th of July or was it after that incident?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: It was after the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that, "The Bosnian army had advanced in that area," can you confirm that there was fighting in that area between two armies?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That is probably the case, but I wasn't present so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm, Mr. Mehonic, whether in the part of Dobrinja in which you lived, if there was fighting in the surroundings of Dobrinja and does that involve Ilidza, Lukavica and Igman, and was it possible to hear armed conflict in Dobrinja and fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that day when you went to the house where people were waiting for water and where the well was located, can you tell us whether you know who owned that house, who lived in that house?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were sitting with a man whom you knew and you also said that, when my learned colleague asked you a question, you said that this person was Taslaman Enver?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether he was waiting in the line for water or did he have some kind of duty?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No. He had some sort of duty. He had to maintain order in the line or something like that. What do I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said you were sitting?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Crouching, that is what I said because there was nothing for me to sit on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, you said you were crouching. Could you tell us whether there were other people in the yard?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were people who collecting water and people who had collected water. They would take turns. There were some who would come and others who would go, that is why this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there were young people in the yard who were sitting there and playing cards?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Not in the yard, but in the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how old these young people were?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Well, about -- they were born in 1950, I would say, something like that. Girls and boys. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you were there, did you notice whether there were any soldiers who were waiting in the line?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, could you tell us how the BH army was dressed, do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that, in response to a question from my learned colleague, you told us that on that day it was sunny and that after the incident, it rained?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was it raining while you were there, too?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I said that it started raining after the incident. Afterwards, I was in a state of shock and I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection on the basis of what you can remember, you told us that after you had found out that your family had died, you told us that you were in a state of a shock. On the basis of your -- of what you can remember, can you tell us again whether there were people who died in the yard?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After you left the hospital, did you try to find out where the shell fell?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And there is still a trace in the street, there is a hole in the street, in the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you can confirm that on the 12th of July, the shell that had exploded made a crater in the street?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a hole at the site where the shell exploded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that that shell exploded in the street then?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I am claiming. And this can be proved. Whoever wants to see this can go and see it for himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Given that you told us that you know that at the site where the shell fell a trace was left, did you find out which direction that shell came from?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the place where the waterline was, was in Kvadrant C.

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement which you gave to the investigators for the Prosecution, you said that, when speaking about that incident, in the continuation of your statement which I have read out to you, when you spoke about the lines that were 50 metres away, you said that the closest position held by the Serbs was called Kvadrant C?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: All of this came under Kvadrant C, but it was towards Nedzarici. The positions were closer to that. There was a well there but it dried up so we were a bit further away from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: You said that the building you lived in was 500 or 600 metres from the place where you were waiting for water?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, something like that. I didn't measure it but I think that it is approximately something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that, when my learned colleague asked you a question, you said that the building in which you lived was shelled. I think that you said it was shelled on seven occasions?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and one woman was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us during which period this building was shelled, in the year 1992, 1993 or 1994?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Well, it was more or less in 1993 and 1994. I don't know exactly, but something like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How far were the front lines from your building and the street in which you lived, the front lines where the BH army and the army with the Republika Srpska was?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I didn't measure it but they weren't very far. Well, maybe about a kilometre or so. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "about a kilometre," are you saying that these positions were in Dobrinja or outside of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: In Dobrinja IV.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the front lines of the BH army and the army of Republika Srpska, are you telling us that these were the positions of both armies? Are you telling us that the positions of both armies were one kilometre from your house or just the position of one of the armies?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: You asked me how far the positions of the Serbian army were from my house. I can't tell you how far the position of the Bosnian army was from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was the BH army anywhere in the vicinity in the house or the street in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993 and 1994, were you able to hear shooting in that part of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to determine who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was no question, Mr. Mehonic. It was just Ms. Pilipovic telling us that she had no further questions for you. Mr. Stamp, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just one area, if I am permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said there is an asphalt -- I beg your pardon, you said there is an impact trace of a shell in the asphalt in front of the gate of the premises of where this tragedy occurred; is that correct? Mr. Mehonic? May I repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear Mr. Stamp, Mr. Mehonic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are asking me this question, I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is a shell impact mark on the asphalt near the gate where the tragedy occurred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I can't hear you very well at all and I can't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some -- could we perhaps just change --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also have problems hearing Mr. Stamp. It is not always very clear. I don't know whether this is purely a technical problem or whether there is some other problem. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hearing Mr. Stamp is one thing, but hearing the translation in your earphones is another thing. Could you perhaps, Mr. Usher, see whether a change of earphones would be of any help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mehonic, could you please tell me whether you can hear the translation of my words well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all that well, but at least a bit better than before now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think these are the few last questions, so would you please try to concentrate and see what you can hear. If you have any difficulties in hearing the questions, then please tell me so that we will see what we can do about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear very well and that means that I don't really understand the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Stamp, you could also use a language which -- such that the witness will not only hear the language, but also understand the language -- the questions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For a moment I thought the Court was inviting me to try out B/C/S, but I think I should just ask the questions more simply. I am guided by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am quite sure that even the subtleties of your language will be translated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is an impact, a shell impact site, near the gate where the tragedy occurred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is on the asphalt surface of the road?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you spent some time in the hospital. Can you recall how long?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: About eight days. Because there were no spare beds and I had to go home, even though I was still sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With the Court's leave, could I ask the usher to hand to the witness P1517C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at that document about seven lines from the top, can you tell us about when you were discharged from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: It must be written somewhere. I can't see anything. I can't find it on this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we might have another translation difficulty here which perhaps we might have to recify after this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp, I am afraid that you are confronted with a problem which is not entirely new to us. Would you be able to ask the witness whether he could show the document he has brought, as he told us, or whether it is still in his possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you have the original document in your possession, Mr. Mehonic, and if you do, could we have a look at it, please?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Well, it is not here at the moment. It is where I am staying at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you be willing to bring it here tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you were discharged about eight days later?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yeah, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When that shell of the 12th of July, 1993, exploded, did you see where it landed yourself? Did you see at that time where it landed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After you were discharged from the hospital, you were shown the impact site on the asphalt?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall about how long after the incident of the 12th of July, 1993, that you were shown that impact site on the asphalt?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: About a month later, because I couldn't walk. I was on crutches.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Nothing further. I would, though, subject to the Court, of course, suggest and propose that the witness be subject to be recalled tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mehonic, Judge Nieto-Navia has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Mehonic, I will read the question and the answer you gave to the Chamber. The question was: "Could you tell us how far you were, how far your flat was from the place you went to collect water?" And the answer was: "100 metres." After that, you said "500 or 600 metres." Which is the correct answer?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Between 500 and 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NEITO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mehonic, you have given answers to all the questions put to you until now. Nevertheless, the Prosecution has asked whether you could come back tomorrow and I --

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would ask you to bring tomorrow the discharge letter we have been speaking about today, of which a copy has been shown to you. But could you bring the discharge letter as it has been given to you and as you told is in your possession? I do understand that it is in the place where you live in The Hague here and not in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM MEHONIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please bring that document with you if you come back tomorrow and that would then be at a quarter past 2.00 tomorrow in the afternoon? I don't think it will take much time, but there might be some additional questions, perhaps in relation to this document. So, therefore, you are not finally excused yet. We expect you to come back tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00. But for today, this is the end of your examination as a witness. So we hope to see you back tomorrow, and for this moment, you are excused. Yes, Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness, Mr. Mehonic, out of the courtroom. I hope to see you back tomorrow, Mr. Mehonic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for until a quarter past 6.00, and may I take it that all preparations will be made as far as the voice distortion, especially, require, so that we can start immediately at a quarter past 6.00. We will adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 6.16 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may just take the opportunity to apologise for being a couple of minutes late. We were trying to clarify the issue in respect to the translation of the document just now, which we have. I don't know if it will be dealt with now or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could just briefly explain so I can sleep better tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The hospital gave the witness a copy when he was discharged or around that time, and a couple years later, I think there are translation problems --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we cannot hear Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I noticed that again and again, there seems to be some problem with your microphone. I am not suggesting the order. Could you perhaps change place or microphones, and perhaps if you also come a bit closer to the microphone that might be helpful as well. I never hear it because you have a loud voice, so even without the earphones, I would hear what you have to say. That is, of course, not true, for those who are dependentant on the technique. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. The witness obtained one copy and the hospital retained one copy which was subsequently delivered to us in 1995 or 1996. When it was delivered to us, the date of this discharge was added. So the original translation had that date which doesn't appear on the copy which he got in 1993 when he was discharged. This is what I am told is the reason for the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The original is going to be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then without a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Without that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Prosecution by tomorrow will determine whether or not we would be in a position to tender the one that we originally obtained from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's deal with it tomorrow. I think that is the best way to do it. It is good that we have this discussion in the absence of the witness. Then we just received a letter. Let me just... It is a letter of Mr. Piletta-Zanin and I see signed in the elegant French language. I see that it is about documents. I think it would be wise first to see what answer will be given to the questions of Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Did the break give the parties the opportunity to clarify the issue of the documents we were talking about before? I think it was your case manager, Mr. Stamp, who would assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am afraid that they did not succeed in clarifying that issue of documents, but that could be done at the end of the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say it was caused by lack of time rather than not being able to...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We haven't been shown the documents yet. We would expect the documents would be shown to us by the Defence so that we could sort through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, those are the documents that I had shown to my learned friend yesterday. I mentioned that the ones that followed, the papers that followed were not a part of that document, and in as far as the document itself is concerned, there was no continuity and of course I expect an answer, quite simply. And the letter in question that you have in front of you, Mr. President, generally speaking, should not even have been submitted to you. But since the Prosecution always keeps submitting these papers to you, I can't help having to clarify. I thought it was a matter that could be settled between the Defence and the Prosecution. As far as I can tell, inasfar as this particular document is concerned, the documents or the elements that would be useful to us would be other elements, for example, R00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not repeat. I would like to hear by tomorrow in the afternoon whether you are able to -- there seems to be to some extent no communication, to some extent also perhaps a bit. Give it another try tomorrow in the afternoon and see whether you can solve it or not. If not, we will further deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite, Mr. President. Perhaps during the break, because we are now almost at the end of the hearing, perhaps the oral answer which should have been given to us during the day could be given to us, that is to say with reference to the dates. And would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reference to the dates. I am afraid I do not exactly understand what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Mr. President, that you have mentioned that the Prosecution could let us know as of tomorrow or, rather, as of today about some answers such as when the Prosecution was informed of the fact that the shrapnel, whatever, would no longer be admissible, and we wanted to know whether this deadline until tomorrow be satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The letter indicating that the shrapnel had not been located was dated the 25th of October, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is when you finally found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We would have received it within a short time after that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The date of receipt is not yet clarified but it would have been within a week after that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you were informed that it was not available?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, not available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to understand something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to thank the Prosecution, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stamp, the Prosecution is ready to call the next witness? That would be a protected witness, as far as I understand, with a pseudonym "Q" and voice and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is everything effective at this moment? One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Usher, would you please lead the witness into the courtroom and may I remind the parties to switch off your microphones. For you perhaps not a big difference, today, Mr. Stamp, but to put off Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your microphones when the witness is answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could I proceed or is there something so urgent as to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Q, because that is how I will call you and that is how everyone will call you in this courtroom, Mr. Q, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Q, before giving testimony in this court, and you will give testimony in this court not recognisable for the outside world because neither your name is used, nor your face can be seen, nor your original voice can be heard, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of the declaration will be given to you now by the usher, and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Q.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Q, you will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness Q, with the leave of the court, I shall hand you a document and I am going to ask you to look at it and then I will ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I, with your leave, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document P3680 [Real-time transcript read in error "P368"].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, you may fold it over now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see your name on that document, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you see your date of birth on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the sake of the transcript, the paper I got in front of me is 3680 and that is not what we can read in the transcript. I know that it is going to be re-read and checked once again, but for the sake of clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the transcript only says 368 and it is 3680. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you a police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you live in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you become a police officer? You could just tell us the month and the year.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: In August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And after you became a police officer, in what city did you work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have any special responsibilities as a police officer and, if so, could you briefly tell us the nature of those responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I worked at the criminal police service, at the security service. So my job was the investigations once a crime had been committed. In 1993, I finished a special course to qualify for that job and so I started to work officially, as I said, in the month that I started my career as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was your profession, if any, before you became a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Student, and I had my own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you have any special duties when you began to work as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What part would you play in the investigations of crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: For the most part, I was involved in cases in Novi Grad, which was the area where I lived, and I worked in the Centar as well as bit. The municipalities of Centar and Novo Sarajevo, so those were the municipalities that I worked in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What type of cases were you involved in investigating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: All cases where there was any reason to start criminal proceedings. So whenever there was a crime such as a burglary, a killing, arson, whenever a crime was involved, we had to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said, "we." Did you work with other police officers in the investigations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Obviously, of course I worked with other police officers because I was not the only member of any team. Any investigation team or inquiry was made up of a judge, other police officers, experts and I, myself, as a forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, what was the normal procedures that you would apply or that would be applied in gathering a team and proceeding and beginning an investigation of a crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Well, as soon as any crime was reported, I took my equipment, the equipment which was necessary for the purposes of the investigation, and then I would wait for the entire team to assemble at a certain spot, at a meeting point. Generally speaking, some people were not necessarily from the same area where I was on duty. For example, a judge or an inspector or somebody else might have come from downtown if we talk about crimes in my own area. So I would wait for them at the police station, the one that was the Centar or where the public security services were situated, and once they got there, we would go to the scene. Upon our arrival at the scene of the crime, we would investigate the situation, and uniformed policemen as a rule should have been there beforehand and they would have had to organise security so as to prevent anyone tampering with any proof, material proof. Upon our arrival, we would examine the crime scene. Then further actions were undertaken, depending on the case in point. For example, we would draw a sketch of the crime scene and then we would take measurements and take pictures and the pictures would be marked adequately, and then we would collect any samples of possible proof which was then packaged and sent off to laboratories for further tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As a forensic expert, did your task at the crime scene involve collecting samples and taking photographs of the scene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did it involve anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: My job was to inspect the scene, take pictures, make the drawings, collect samples and send them off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, can you recall the 22nd of January, 1994? Did you investigate an incident which occurred at Alipasino Polje on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. I do remember that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In January 1994, which district -- you need not tell us the address, which district did you live in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I used to live in Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said your normal police working area was Novi Grad. Did that include Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Alipasino Polje is a direct in Novi Grad, a settlement in Novi Grad. It is a part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, where were you when you first heard of the incident which occurred on the 22nd of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I was in the premises of the security services station in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you, along with a team, go to Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you arrived at Alipasino Polje, did you conduct an investigation, and if so, can you tell us what you observed and what you did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: When we arrived on the site, I saw that two shells had fallen in front of the buildings at a distance of about 20 metres perhaps. There was a lot of blood and traces of tissue in the vicinity of the explosion. At the site where the explosion occurred in Klara Zetkin Street, there was a sleigh near the explosion and near that sleigh, there was traces of tissue and there was quite a bit of it, whereas the traces of blood were more visible at the site where the explosion occurred in Cetinska Street. When we arrived at the location, I noticed -- I only noticed the traces of one of the shells because we didn't immediately go to the site after the explosion. We waited for the whole team to assemble. What happened to the traces of the second shell, we don't know because when we arrived at the site, we didn't notice any traces of that second shell. I took some photographs --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean by, "traces of a shell"? What traces are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: The main trace that a shell leaves is its stabiliser, it's a mortar shell, and this was the case. And I found one such stabiliser. And there was shrapnel that could be found in the immediate vicinity, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said one shell fell at Klara Zetkin Street and another at Cetinska Street. Could you describe those streets and the area around which the shells fell.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: That is a residential area, so those two streets, Cetinska and Klara Street, join up at a crossroads and they form of a sort of round about, a circular road which encircles the entire settlement. Next to those streets there are buildings with several floors. In fact, there are skyscrapers of ten stories and behind those buildings there is a grass area or, rather, a park. The Klara Zetkin Street and Cetinska are open for traffic, whereas it's a pedestrian area between the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall about how far apart the two shells, one which fell on Klara Zetkin and the other on Cetinska Street, were, how far apart these two shells fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: You are referring to the time? A few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, a few minutes, but I was referring to the distance between the two shells. Can you say approximately how far it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Between -- well, about 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you took photographs of the scene. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive information, and from your observation I take it you would have concluded that there were casualties from this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: As a result of the explosion of that shell, six children died and several people were wounded. I couldn't provide you with an exact number because the information on the wounded was gathered subsequently because the wounded were taken to the first -- to the closest hospitals and to the closest emergency services. So other members of the investigatative teams would carry that out. I received information a little after the investigation itself was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said "as a result of explosion," as if singular. One explosion, six children died. Did the children die from -- as a result of one explosion or both explosions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I carried out one investigation which concerned two explosions. Whether they died because of both explosions -- well, after the investigation had been carried out, I found out -- I determined that six children had died. Whether they died because of both of the explosions or because of one of them, I don't know. But my investigation related to both explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in respect to the photograph that he said that he took, I beg to tender to him Exhibit P2172. I believe it is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least in your list it appears, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before it is put anywhere -- very well. I just would remind the usher that the front part of the document is under seal and should not be shown on the cameras.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
